property_summary: For any callee address that reverts on receiving Ether, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract C forwards the withdrawal through withdraw(uint) which uses .transfer and thus bubbles the revert (so the contract balance remains unchanged), whereas the mutant that directly does payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) will attempt the transfer to msg.sender immediately and thus also revert — the general rule we assert is that after calling withdrawAll as the owner, C's balance becomes zero iff the owner contract successfully receives funds; using an adversarial owner that reverts will keep C's balance unchanged in the reference but the mutant may behave differently for some fuzzed deposit amounts and adversary behaviors (we target a reverter owner to distinguish behavior).

For any depositor amount and any owner address that may be a normal EOA or a contract, if withdrawAll is invoked by the owner then the reference C always routes the withdrawal through withdraw(uint) (which uses transfer to msg.sender) so the contract balance becomes zero exactly when the transfer to the owner succeeds; the mutant that directly does payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can behave differently when the owner is a contract that re-enters during receive (re-entrant owner) because the direct single transfer bypasses the withdraw(uint) call path and can allow the owner to re-enter and disturb balances — hence there exist fuzzed inputs (deposit amounts and an adversarial re-entrant owner) where the reference keeps invariant (no re-entrancy during withdraw path) but the mutant does not, which the test detects by asserting address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll by the owner for all admissible inputs in the reference but failing for the mutant for some inputs.

For any owner and any deposited amount, when the owner (which may be a contract) calls withdrawAll the reference C always routes the payout through withdraw(uint) so the contract balance becomes zero iff the transfer to the owner succeeds; the mutant that directly does payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can be distinguished because a re-entrant owner contract can manipulate control-flow during a single direct transfer causing the final contract balance to remain non-zero for some deposit amounts and adversarial owner behavior.

For any nonzero deposit amount and any owner address, if the owner calls withdrawAll then the reference contract C always results in address(c).balance == 0 (it withdraws via withdraw(uint)), while the mutant that directly transfers the whole balance to msg.sender can be made to leave a nonzero balance for some adversarial owner contract that re-enters (so the invariant fails for some inputs).

For any owner and any deposit amount, when the owner calls withdrawAll the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it withdraws via withdraw(uint) which transfers the full balance); the mutant that replaces that call with a direct transfer can leave a nonzero contract balance for some adversarial owner contracts that revert on receive, so the invariant (address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll by owner) holds for the reference for all inputs but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

Only the contract owner can successfully call withdrawAll (so after any caller calls withdrawAll, the contract balance remains unchanged unless caller is the owner); the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner caller to drain the contract, violating this property for some fuzzed caller and amount.

For every caller and deposit amount, only the owner can drain the contract via withdrawAll — so after any non-owner calls withdrawAll the contract balance remains unchanged; the mutant removing the onlyOwner check allows a non-owner to successfully withdraw and reduce the contract balance for some fuzzed caller/amount.

For any recipient address that reverts on receiving funds, the reference contract's withdraw will always revert (so the call fails and contract balance stays unchanged), while the mutated version that uses call{value:...} may observe a different revert/accept outcome; specifically, when the recipient's fallback reverts, the reference (which used transfer) will also revert, but the mutant's different gas/behavior can make the outcome differ — thus the invariant is that withdraw to a reverting recipient always fails on the reference but can behave differently on the mutant.

For any recipient that accepts plain transfers (i.e., whose receive() does not revert and does not consume excessive gas), calling withdraw(x) as owner always reduces C's balance by x (succeeds) on the reference implementation; the mutant that replaces transfer with call can fail to transfer (or behave differently) for some recipient behaviours/amounts, so there exist inputs where withdraw does not succeed and C's balance does not decrease.

For any recipient contract that accepts plain transfers (i.e. its receive() is non-reverting and uses small gas), when the owner calls withdraw(amount) the reference C (which uses transfer) always succeeds and reduces C's balance by exactly that amount; the mutant that replaces transfer with a raw call can, for some recipient behaviors/amounts, fail to transfer and thus not reduce C's balance.

For every nonzero withdraw amount sent by the owner to any recipient that ACCEPTS funds (has a payable receive/fallback that does not revert), the correct contract always reduces C's balance by that amount after withdraw; the mutant replacing transfer with call can fail for some recipient behaviors/amounts, so there exist inputs where C's balance does not decrease.

For any owner-initiated withdraw of amount A to a recipient that deliberately consumes all gas in its receive() (but does not revert), the reference C using transfer always succeeds and reduces C's balance by A, while the mutant using call can fail to transfer (or behave differently) for some A/recipient, so there exist fuzzed inputs where the mutant does not reduce C's balance though the reference always would.

Invariant: Only the contract owner can withdraw Ether from the contract; the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner to withdraw and thus change contract balance for some inputs (fuzzed caller and amount).

For all callers and amounts, only the deployer (owner) can successfully withdraw funds from C (so non-owners cannot reduce address(c).balance); the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction allowing some non-owner caller/amount to reduce address(c).balance and thus violate this rule.

For any caller who is the owner, calling withdraw(...) succeeds and decreases the contract balance by the withdrawn amount; the mutant inverts ownership check causing owner calls to revert (or not transfer) for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller equal to the owner and any withdraw amount ≤ contract balance, calling withdraw succeeds and reduces address(c).balance by that amount; the mutant inverts onlyOwner and thus causes owner calls to revert (or not transfer) for some inputs.

For any non-owner caller, withdraw(...) must revert (only owner may succeed); the mutant inverts the check so some non-owner calls that should revert may succeed, causing a differing post-call balance/behavior.
For every caller and amount, when the contract owner calls withdraw(amount) the call must succeed (not revert) — the mutant flips onlyOwner causing owner calls to revert for some inputs.

For any caller address A and any amount X (0 <= X <= address(c).balance) if A is the contract owner then calling withdraw(X) must succeed (not revert) and leave address(c).balance decreased by X; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so an owner call can revert — the test asserts the call succeeds (ok == true) for owner calls and thus will fail on the mutant for some fuzzed inputs.

For any target and value, when the target's fallback reverts, the reference contract's sendMoney returns (call returns false) without reverting the whole transaction (so sendMoney call succeeds and depositsCount/state remains unchanged), whereas the mutant using transfer will always revert when the callee reverts; thus the reference never reverts for a reverting callee but the mutant can revert for some inputs.

For any target address and amount, calling sendMoney on the correct contract never reverts when the callee's fallback reverts (the low-level call returns false but sendMoney itself returns normally), whereas the mutant using transfer will revert for some target/amount when the callee reverts; therefore the reference always completes (ok == true) while the mutant can fail (ok == false) for a reverting callee.

For any target contract with a payable fallback that MAY revert when receiving funds, the reference C never reverts from sendMoney (it catches failure of the low-level call and returns), so after calling sendMoney the invocation itself always completes (ok == true); the mutant using transfer can revert for some targets/amounts causing the call to fail (ok == false).

For any target and value where the target's fallback/receive consumes gas but does NOT revert (e.g. a contract that uses up gas and then returns), the reference C's sendMoney (using low-level call) will complete successfully (no revert) while the mutant using transfer may revert due to gas stipend limitations — so the property: calling sendMoney on such a gas-eating but non-reverting target always returns (ok == true) for the reference C, but the mutant can fail for some fuzzed amounts/targets.

For any target address and amount, calling sendMoney on the correct contract either forwards the funds successfully (call returns true) or reverts so the caller observes failure; the mutant swallows a failing call and thus can make sendMoney appear successful even when the external call would have failed (i.e., correct contract never silently ignores a failed external call, mutant can).
